This page exists because a study plan that does not say what it is aiming at is a hobby. Everything here is
about the thing the other 365 pages are for: a seat as a **buy-side quantitative researcher**, applied for
during 2027.

The last section is the uncomfortable one and it is the reason to read this in September rather than in
June, because two of the gaps take a year to close and one of them you close by choosing differently.

## The seat you are aiming at

**Quantitative researcher, systematic equity or multi-asset.** You are given data, a research platform and
a mandate, and you produce signals that go into a book someone else risks capital on. The work is
statistics under adversarial conditions: the effects are small, the data is non-stationary, most of what
you find is not real, and the cost of being wrong is measured rather than argued about.

That description is not a coincidence. It is the seat where your existing training transfers hardest, and
the mapping is specific:

| What you do now | What it is called there |
|:--|:--|
| Mendelian randomization | Instrumental variable estimation |
| Genome-wide significance, winner's curse | Backtest overfitting, the deflated Sharpe ratio |
| Colocalization | Bayesian model comparison over shared-signal hypotheses |
| Conditioning an LD matrix | Shrinking a return covariance matrix |
| Not splitting relatives across folds | Purged, embargoed cross-validation |
| Ascertainment bias in a cohort | Survivorship bias in a universe |

Four adjacent seats you will see advertised, and how they differ:

- **Quantitative trader.** Faster horizons, more decisions per day, and the interview is a trading game
  rather than a research presentation. Weeks 41–44 and 49 are the parts of this course that point here.
- **Quantitative developer.** Building the platform rather than the signals. Better paid at the entry
  level, harder to move out of into research than people expect. Phase 10 is the relevant preparation and
  it is not enough on its own.
- **Quantitative analyst, sell side.** Derivatives pricing and risk at a bank. More mathematics, less
  data, much less of your existing training used. Phase 8 is the relevant preparation.
- **Data scientist at a systematic manager.** Sometimes the same job with a different title and sometimes
  a support function. Ask, in the first call, whose profit and loss the work appears in.

## Who hires, and what the structure does to the job

Four structures, and the difference matters more than the brand:

**Multi-manager pod shops** — Millennium, Point72, Balyasny, Citadel's equities business. A portfolio
manager runs a book, you are on their team, and the drawdown limit is real and short. Fastest entry,
fastest exit, and the highest variance in outcome. Ask what happens to the team if the book is down 5
percent.

**Partnerships and prop firms** — Jane Street, Optiver, IMC, SIG, Hudson River. Trade their own capital,
no external investors, longer horizons on people. The bar at entry is the highest and the interview is the
most standardised, which is good for you because a standardised process rewards preparation.

**Systematic managers** — AQR, Man AHL, Winton, Two Sigma, D. E. Shaw. Research at longer horizons,
published papers, closest to what you have spent this year doing and the closest cultural match to
academia. Slowest hiring, smallest number of seats.

**Bank quant groups.** Different work, mentioned for completeness. Better hours, lower ceiling.

## The process, round by round

Roughly five stages over four to eight weeks, and each one is testing something different:

1. **Screen.** CV against a filter, human or otherwise. This is where the genetics background is either a
   differentiator or a reason to stop reading, and which one it is depends entirely on the vocabulary on
   the first page. Day 351 is about that.
2. **Online test.** Timed probability and mathematics, often an hour, often unforgiving. This round has no
   partial credit and no conversation, and it is the one the drill thread exists for. Fifty sittings of
   twenty minutes is the preparation; four weeks in July is not.
3. **Technical phone screens.** One to three of them. Probability out loud, statistics, coding, and for a
   research seat a conversation about something you built. The failure mode here is length, not
   correctness — week 50 is entirely about compressing correct answers into ninety seconds.
4. **The superday.** Four to six back-to-back rounds: probability under a clock, a trading or estimation
   game, a coding round, your research presentation, and one behavioural conversation. Nobody tells you
   which is next. Day 355 exists because the transitions are what actually degrade.
5. **Offer and negotiation.** Day 356. The short version: the sign-on and any first-year guarantee move,
   the base moves within a band, the deferral schedule does not, and the leverage comes entirely from
   having a second process finishing at the same time.

**What each round is really testing.** The probability rounds test whether you can be quantitative under
time pressure with someone watching, which is a different skill from being quantitative. The research
presentation tests whether you know which of your results is weakest. The trading game tests whether you
update on evidence when the evidence is that someone chose to trade with you. None of these are tests of
what you know.

## Timing

- **Autumn 2026 through spring 2027** — no applications. You have nothing to show yet and a rejection now
  costs you the same firm later.
- **March–April 2027** — the firm list and the outreach for conversations rather than roles ([day
  353](days/day-353.qmd), [day 354](days/day-354.qmd)). Referrals take months to become anything and this
  is the last point at which starting them still works.
- **May–July 2027** — applications, in a batch rather than sequentially. Batching is what gives you two
  offers in the same fortnight, and two offers in the same fortnight is the only real negotiating
  position that exists.
- **August–October 2027** — processes run. Expect four to eight weeks each and expect several to end
  without explanation.

Two calendar facts worth knowing: the campus pipelines these firms run for graduating PhDs fill in the
autumn for the following summer, and you are not in that pipeline. Experienced-hire processes run
continuously and are less predictable but also less seasonal, which is the route you are on.

## The honest gaps

**You are a career changer, and the default pipeline is not built for you.** The standard hire is a PhD in
physics, mathematics or computer science, recruited in their final year through a campus process, with no
industry experience and no expectation of any. You are a postdoc in a different field applying laterally.
That is not disqualifying and it does mean every application is a non-standard one, which raises the value
of a referral from a low multiple to the single largest factor in the outcome.

**You have no track record anyone can verify.** A paper-traded year is not a track record and will not be
treated as one. What it is is evidence of process, which is a different and still useful thing. The two
public records that carry actual weight are a Numerai history with real submissions over time ([day
230](days/day-230.qmd)) and a placing in a serious competition. Both take months of elapsed time, which is
why they are in the course early rather than in phase 11.

**Madison is not where these jobs are.** They are in New York, Chicago, London, and a small number in the
Bay Area, Amsterdam and Hong Kong. Remote research seats exist and are rare and mostly go to people with
an existing track record at the firm. Decide before you apply whether you will move, because the answer
changes the firm list and it is a question you will be asked in the first call.

**The competition is specifically good at the interview.** The pool includes people who have been doing
timed competitive mathematics since they were sixteen and who will beat you on the online test on speed
alone. The drill thread is the only response to that and it works by accumulating fifty sittings rather
than by intensity.

**Your background reads as biology to a screener.** This is the gap you close cheapest and it is entirely
a vocabulary problem. "Genome-wide association study of protein levels" and "high-dimensional multiple
testing with a controlled error rate across 10 million correlated hypotheses" describe the same work, and
only one of them survives a thirty-second CV scan by someone hiring for statistical arbitrage.

**You will not be a C++ programmer in a year.** Phase 10 gets you to reading a matching engine and writing
something small that works. That is a real and defensible claim and it is not the same as the claim a
low-latency firm needs. It closes the quantitative developer route and closes most of high-frequency
trading, and both of those were closed anyway for reasons that have nothing to do with C++.

**The base rate is against any individual application, and that is the wrong frame.** The relevant
questions are how many processes you can run in parallel, how many are warm rather than cold, and whether
what you can show is different from what everyone else shows. You control all three. Nobody applying from
a physics PhD arrives with instrumental variables and massive multiple testing already in their hands, and
that is the entire argument for this year.

**One year at an hour a day is not a PhD in this field.** By August 2027 you will be able to hold a
research conversation, build a defensible backtest, derive Black-Scholes and pass a probability round.
There are people three years into the seat you want who have forgotten more market structure than this
course covers. The plan is to be hireable, not to be finished.

## What actually changes the outcome

In rough order of effect:

1. **A referral.** One warm introduction is worth more than twenty applications, and warm introductions
   come from conversations started months earlier about something specific the person worked on.
2. **A work product someone can read in ten minutes.** The three two-page write-ups from [milestone
   11](milestones.qmd#m357). Almost nobody applying has one, and it converts a screening decision from a
   guess into a reading.
3. **The drill thread, finished.** Not started in June. The online test has no partial credit and the
   probability round is the most common single point of failure for exactly the kind of candidate you are.
4. **Being able to say what is weakest in your own work.** [Milestone 9](milestones.qmd#m308) requires you
   to name an earlier result you now believe was wrong. That habit is the most distinguishing thing you
   can bring into a research conversation, and it is rarer than it should be.

## If it does not work in 2027

Three outcomes that are not failure, listed because deciding in advance which of them you would accept
stops the decision being made under pressure in November:

- **An adjacent seat with a path.** A quantitative developer or data science role at a systematic manager,
  moving into research from inside. Slower, and internal moves have a much higher success rate than
  external applications.
- **Applying again in 2028 with a live track record.** A second year of the paper account, or a real one,
  plus a Numerai history with two years of submissions, is a materially different application from the
  2027 one.
- **Running your own capital and not changing jobs.** Everything in this course works at small size, and
  the strategies with capacity too small for a fund to bother with are the ones you can actually run. The
  [capstone](days/day-365.qmd) asks what you would run with your own money and at what size, and a
  serious answer to that question is worth having regardless of what happens to the applications.
